newsitem.title: USA: Canadian official critical of U.S. moves on Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Canadian official critical of U.S. moves on Cuba.

text.p: Canada's foreign minister said on Friday that U.S. efforts to defend its economic sanctions on communist Cuba could subvert the World Trade Organisation and slow global economic progress.

Lloyd Axworthy said the U.S. Helms-Burton law has resulted in "almost a contradiction in goals" for the United States. The law, passed last year after Cuban jets shot down two planes operated by a Miami-based exile group, seeks to punish foreign companies who do business with properties confiscated after Fidel Castro came to power.

Axworthy, speaking at the Chicago Council on Foreign Relations, said U.S. plans to defend Helms-Burton -- possibly by claiming it as a national security exemption -- to the World Trade Organisation were dangerous.

"Because if the United States can claim national security why can't other countries? ... all of a sudden everyone is claiming exemptions to a rule they don't like, and all of a sudden that carefully constructed economic architecture that is really the framework within which there can be enormous expansion and acceleration of trade and investment is called into question.
"There's a virus put in the system that I think has to be dealt with," he said.
The 2-year-old WTO is designed to open world markets by settling protectionist questions.
Canada has maintained good relations with Castro's government while the United States has kept an embargo against the island nation for 35 years.

Axworthy, who last month became the most senior Canadian official to visit Cuba in two decades, said a declaration signed by both countries is a "work in progress" that should yield concrete progress for human rights and other issues.
He said Canadian officials would soon begin discussions in Cuba on various human rights questions and would hold a conference in April on the rights of women and children.
He also said there is evidence that Cuba is interested in joining an anti-terrorism compact.

"It was a major step forward," Axworthy told reporters following his speech to the council. "It is the first time the Cubans have ever signed such a document with any other country, where they were prepared to address these issues ... certainly we didn't see it at any time as a one-stop venture."
